title: Persuasion Under the Surface
theme: Persuasive techniques: how messages move people
objectives: I can name and explain persuasive techniques such as slogans, testimonials, and incentives.
I can describe how word choice, connotation, and exaggeration change the way a message feels.
I can tell the difference between a compelling message and a deceptive or sensational one.
I can use the endings -ive, -al, -ial, and -ing to understand describing words.
rationale: Seventh graders meet ads, endorsements, and slogans every day, but few can name what those messages are doing. This unit supplies the vocabulary for persuasive techniques (slogan, testimonial, incentive, endorse, sway) and for the qualities of persuasive language (connotation, deceptive, sensational, compelling), with propaganda as the larger-scale case. Students use the words in a low-stakes setting, a cereal box, before they apply them to speeches, news, and online posts. Fallacy and rebut return from the argument unit so students can respond to a persuasive message, and distract returns from the tract unit as a technique advertisers use.

words.def: The feeling or idea a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.
words.ex: The word cheap has a negative connotation, while affordable sounds more positive.
words.ex2: Writers choose words with care because even synonyms can have very different connotations.
words.nonExample: A word's dictionary definition is its literal meaning, not its connotation.

apps.academic: A poet may pick a word for its connotation rather than its literal meaning.
apps.spoken: Calling someone stubborn has a different connotation than calling them determined.
apps.writing: Use connotation when you discuss the feeling a word creates, not its definition.

misuse.s: The connotation of a word is its exact dictionary meaning, and it never includes any feeling.
misuse.why: Connotation is the feeling a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.

words.def: A short, catchy phrase used to make people remember a product, group, or cause.
words.ex: The campaign's slogan, Clean Streets, Bright Future, appeared on every poster in town.
words.ex2: A good slogan can be said in four seconds and remembered for forty years.

apps.academic: In media class, we compared the slogans of three different brands.
apps.spoken: That slogan is so catchy that I can't stop humming it.
apps.writing: Use slogan for a short phrase, and describe its sound or word choice to explain why it works.

cloze2.s: Because the ___ rhymed and was only four words long, children repeated it on the playground.

misuse.s: A slogan is a three-page report that explains every fact about a product in detail.

words.def: To publicly say that you support or approve of a person, product, or idea.
words.ex: The mayor endorsed the plan to build a new bike path along the river.
words.ex2: A famous chef will not endorse a restaurant unless she has eaten there herself.
words.nonExample: Quietly doubting a product and saying nothing is not endorsing it.

apps.academic: A newspaper may endorse a candidate, and readers should ask why.
apps.spoken: Would you endorse that brand, or are you just trying it?
apps.writing: Use endorse when someone puts their name or reputation behind a choice.

cloze.s: The senator agreed to ___ the candidate at the rally, telling the crowd she was the best choice.

cloze2.s: Companies sometimes pay celebrities to ___ their products in television commercials.

misuse.s: The mayor endorsed the plan by loudly telling everyone that she opposed it and would vote against it.
misuse.why: To endorse is to publicly support; saying she opposes it is the opposite.

words.def: One-sided information spread to shape what many people believe, often by hiding facts.
words.ex: During the war, posters full of propaganda urged citizens to see the enemy as a monster.
words.ex2: Students compared a news report with a piece of propaganda and listed which facts the poster left out.
words.nonExample: A balanced article that shows several viewpoints and lists its sources is not propaganda.

apps.academic: Historians study propaganda to see how governments tried to shape public opinion.
apps.spoken: That video felt like propaganda because it only showed one side.
apps.writing: Use propaganda for one-sided messages meant to shape a whole group's beliefs.

cloze2.s: To spot ___, ask who made the message, what it wants you to believe, and what facts it leaves out.

misuse.s: Propaganda is a fair report that presents every side equally and lists all of its sources.

words.def: To influence someone's opinion or decision.

senses.def: To move slowly from side to side.

words.ex: A powerful speech can sway voters who are still undecided.
words.ex2: Her friends tried to sway her into choosing the red jacket, but she stayed with the blue one.

words.def: Something offered to encourage people to do something.
words.ex: The library offered a free book as an incentive for children who finished the reading challenge.
words.ex2: Lower prices after eight o'clock are an incentive to shop when the store is quieter.
words.nonExample: A rule that punishes you is a penalty, not an incentive.

apps.academic: Economists study how an incentive such as a discount changes what people buy.
apps.spoken: What's my incentive for cleaning the garage?
apps.writing: Use incentive for a reward that is offered before the action, not for the result.

cloze.s: The company gave workers a bonus as an ___ to finish the project ahead of schedule.

cloze2.s: A discount coupon is an ___ that makes shoppers more likely to try a new brand.

misuse.s: A fine for littering is a great incentive because it rewards people who drop trash.
misuse.why: An incentive encourages action by offering something; a fine is a penalty, and it does not reward littering.

words.frame: A good incentive for ___ would be ___.

words.def: Giving a false impression; misleading, even if not exactly a lie.
words.ex: The deceptive ad showed a huge burger, but the real one was half the size.
words.ex2: It is deceptive to leave out facts that would change a buyer's mind.
words.nonExample: A label that clearly lists every ingredient and its amount is not deceptive.

apps.academic: Statistics can be deceptive when a graph leaves out part of the scale.
apps.spoken: That price was deceptive; the fees were hidden at the bottom.
apps.writing: Use deceptive for a message that misleads even when each word is technically true.

cloze.s: The price looked low, but the ___ sign hid the extra fees in tiny print.

cloze2.s: Because the photo had been edited to hide the damage, the car's online listing was ___.

misuse.s: The ad was deceptive because it explained each fact clearly and left nothing out.
misuse.why: Deceptive means misleading; explaining everything clearly is the opposite.

visual.alt: A theater mask beside an oversized hamburger.

words.frame: An ad is deceptive when it ___.

words.def: Designed to shock or thrill people, often by exaggerating.

senses.example: The gymnast's sensational routine earned a perfect score.

words.ex: The tabloid ran a sensational headline about a creature in the lake, though there was no evidence.
words.ex2: Some websites use sensational titles to get more clicks, even when the story is ordinary.
words.nonExample: A calm report that sticks to checked facts is not sensational.

apps.academic: Media-literacy classes ask students to spot sensational language in headlines.
apps.spoken: That headline is so sensational that I doubt the story is true.
apps.writing: Use sensational for exaggerated or shocking presentation, not for ordinary excitement.

cloze.s: The newspaper's ___ headline screamed about a shocking secret, but the story inside was ordinary.

cloze2.s: Calm reporters avoid ___ language that makes a small event sound like a disaster.

misuse.s: The sensational report was dull and careful, and it avoided every exaggeration.
misuse.why: Sensational means built to shock or thrill; a dull, careful report is the opposite.

words.frame: A sensational headline tries to ___ instead of ___.

words.def: Strong enough to hold your attention or make you agree.
words.ex: The lawyer made a compelling argument, backed by three clear pieces of evidence.
words.ex2: The documentary was so compelling that no one in the room looked at a phone.
words.nonExample: A speech that bores the audience and offers no evidence is not compelling.

apps.academic: A compelling thesis is clear, specific, and backed by evidence.
apps.spoken: That was a compelling reason, and I changed my mind.
apps.writing: Use compelling for reasons or stories that truly draw readers in.

cloze2.s: Her ___ story kept the entire class silent until the last sentence.

misuse.s: The compelling argument was so weak and confusing that nobody paid attention to it.
misuse.why: A compelling argument holds attention and persuades; a weak, confusing one does not.

passage.title: Reading the Cereal Box
paras: Last week my media class made a list of every message we saw before breakfast. I counted thirty-one. Most were ads, and one cereal box, Crunch Comet, carried five persuasive tricks on its front panel alone. Learning to spot them did not make ads less fun. It just made me harder to sway.

The first trick is the slogan, a short, catchy phrase meant to stick in your mind. Crunch Comet's slogan is "Blast Off Every Morning!" Notice the word blast. Its connotation, the feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning, is energy and excitement. A plain word like eat carries no such feeling, which is why advertisers choose their words with care.

The second trick is the testimonial, a statement from a person praising the product. On the box, a famous skateboarder says, "I never skip Crunch Comet." The company pays him to endorse the cereal, which means he publicly supports it. That does not make him a liar, but it should make us ask whether his opinion is truly independent.

Then there is the incentive, something offered to make you act. Every box hides a collector card, and the front shows a shiny gold card twice as big as the real one. That picture is deceptive: it leaves a false impression without telling an exact lie. Near the cereal aisle, a poster screamed, "SHOCKING TASTE SECRET REVEALED!" That sensational headline was built to thrill, not to inform.

Some persuasion is harmless fun, but propaganda is different. It spreads one-sided messages to shape what many people believe, often by hiding facts. A cereal box is not propaganda, yet it borrows many of the same tools. A message can be compelling without being true; sometimes it is simply well designed. I will keep eating Crunch Comet, but I will read the box like a detective.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "connotation" most nearly means
choices: the feeling a word suggests beyond its meaning
the exact dictionary definition of a word
the number of letters in a word
the first word of a slogan
qs.why: The writer defines it right after the word: the feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning.

qs.q: Why does the writer say the skateboarder's endorsement "does not make him a liar"?
choices: Because skateboarders never tell lies
Because being paid does not prove he is lying, but it may affect how independent his opinion is
Because the cereal box is not an ad
Because the company wrote the quote itself
qs.why: The writer separates two ideas: being paid does not make someone dishonest, yet it is a reason to ask whether the praise is independent.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the picture of the gold card is deceptive?
choices: It is on the front of the box.
It is a collector card.
It is hidden in every box.
It shows the card twice as big as the real one.
qs.why: The enlarged picture creates a false impression of the prize without a spoken lie.

qs.q: The writer calls the headline "sensational" because it is
choices: carefully balanced and calm
written by a famous skateboarder
meant to excite rather than inform
too long to remember
qs.why: The text says it was built to thrill, not to inform.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Cereal is unhealthy and should be avoided.
Naming persuasive techniques helps people read ads more carefully without ruining the fun.
Skateboarders should not appear in ads.
A message is true if it is exciting.
qs.why: The writer says spotting the tricks makes ads no less fun but makes the writer harder to sway, and ends by reading the box like a detective.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for analyzing persuasion, read a student's blog post that picks apart a cereal box, practice the endings -ive, -al, -ial, and -ing, and write short analyses of ads or headlines. The aim is a shared vocabulary, so students can explain how a message works instead of only saying it is good or bad.

notes.va.connotation.n: Pair with denotation (the dictionary meaning). Use synonym pairs such as thrifty and cheap or curious and nosy and have students rank them from positive to negative. Keep the word abstract only as long as examples are concrete.
notes.va.slogan.n: A concrete entry word; students will bring examples. Ask them to explain why a slogan is memorable (rhyme, rhythm, repetition) and what feeling its words carry.
notes.va.endorse.v: Point out the difference between supporting an idea and being paid to support it. Keep the discussion on how readers should evaluate an endorsement, not on specific people or brands.
notes.va.propaganda.n: A heavy word; use historical examples with care and let students analyze a neutral invented poster. The key check: one-sided, aimed at a large group, and hiding or bending facts. A cereal box is not propaganda.
notes.va.sway.v: Multiple meaning: influence versus move side to side. Show the figurative sense as a swaying of the mind. Have students say what evidence would sway them.
notes.va.incentive.n: Link to the economics unit: an incentive changes behavior. Ask students to design an incentive for a school task. Contrast with a penalty.
notes.va.deceptive.adj: Stress that a deceptive message can use only true words yet leave a false impression. Use the burger photo as a model and have students find a graph that is deceptive because of its scale.
notes.va.sensational.adj: Distinguish from the other sense (a sensational performance means wonderful); the unit teaches exaggerated and shocking. Use headlines students write themselves, rewriting one plainly.
notes.va.compelling.adj: Compelling can describe an argument, a story, or a speaker. Ask what makes a reason compelling: evidence, clear logic, and specific detail. Contrast with sensational.
notes.va.testimonial.n: A personal statement used to persuade. Teach students that a testimonial is not proof; ask what evidence would be stronger (a test, data, an independent review).

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The box calls the cereal a blast. Blast has a connotation of energy. The dictionary meaning of blast is an explosion, but nobody thinks the cereal will explode. The word is chosen for the feeling. Then the skateboarder endorses the cereal, which is a testimonial. I need to ask whether the testimonial is proof or only persuasion.'
discuss: Where have you seen a slogan or a testimonial that actually changed your mind, and what made it work?
When does a persuasive message cross from compelling into deceptive?
misconceptions: Propaganda is just another word for advertising.
Connotation and definition mean the same thing.
extend: Collect five ads or headlines and label each with one word from the unit.
Rewrite a sensational headline as a plain one and compare the two.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit deceptive/compelling and sensational/compelling as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week. Ask students to apply fallacy and rebut to a persuasive message (what is the claim, and how would you rebut it), and use distract when discussing how ads pull attention away from missing facts.
